definition: To hide your real feelings, motives, or thoughts behind a false appearance.
example: The ambassador learned to dissemble, hiding his alarm behind a calm and courteous smile.
nuance: Unlike lying outright, dissembling usually hides the truth through a misleading manner; don't confuse it with disassemble.
prompt: A job candidate is asked why she left her last position.
options: Unwilling to admit she had been fired, she began to dissemble, calling it a mutual decision.
She explained that her old job was to dissemble broken printers and sort their parts for recycling.
She decided to dissemble, telling the interviewer exactly why she had been let go.
She hoped her new team would dissemble in the lobby each morning for a quick meeting.
reasons: She covers an embarrassing truth with a misleading story, which is exactly what this verb describes.
Taking machines apart is disassembling; this word is about concealing the truth.
Giving a fully honest answer reveals the truth instead of masking it.
Gathering people together is assembling; the word has nothing to do with meeting up.

practice.prompt: A boy breaks his grandmother's vase while she is out running errands.
options: When she asked about the vase, he tried to dissemble, shrugging as if puzzled.
He grabbed a screwdriver to dissemble the cabinet and sweep up the shards hidden beneath it.
He chose to dissemble, pointing to the shards and confessing the moment she walked in.
The replacement vase she bought will dissemble the old one so closely that no one will notice.
reasons: Pretending to be confused so his guilt stays hidden is a clear case of putting on a false front.
Unscrewing furniture is disassembling, a look-alike word with a completely different meaning.
An immediate confession exposes what happened rather than concealing it.
Looking like something else is resembling; this verb describes a person hiding feelings or motives.
